 San Francisco’s Congressional Earthquake
 By 
 Ed Kilgore ,
 political columnist for Intelligencer since 2015 
 Nov. 19, 2026 
 Save this article to read it later.
 Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section.
 Photo-Illustration: Intelligencer; Photos: Getty Images 
 This year’s contest between Scott Wiener and Connie Chan to succeed Nancy Pelosi as San Francisco’s U.S. representative didn’t get much national attention on Election Night, partly because it was a Democrat-on-Democrat battle (thanks to California’s top-two primary system) and partly because we count votes very slowly in the Golden State. But it’s worth looking back on. The race to represent CA-11 was a fascinating microcosm of the California Democratic Party’s love-hate relationship with the tech community and the still obscure but important internal dynamics of the companies involved in AI. That the story also involves the legendary House Speaker Pelosi (who held this seat for 20 terms) and Wiener, the OG pioneer of the Abundance movement that has swept some Democratic precincts and alarmed others, makes it even more compelling.
 Back in late 2022, Pelosi formally stepped down as Democratic House leader after 20 years (eight of them as Speaker of the House, the other 12 as minority leader). But she chose to remain in Congress for two more terms as potential successors waited for her to announce her retirement.
 State Senator (and former San Francisco supervisor) Scott Wiener was long interested in moving up the ladder to Congress, having already established a statewide and then a national reputation as the author of up-zoning legislation seeking to force local governments in California to accommodate multifamily-housing development instead of endlessly prioritizing the mythic single-family-house-with-a-yard residential land-use pattern. Wiener’s battles with powerful NIMBY forces added to the local fame he had already achieved as a champion of LGBTQ+ rights. Meanwhile, Pelosi was perceived by many observers as keeping her seat warm until her daughter, Christine Pelosi , a political consultant and veteran staffer in both the federal and local governments, was ready to occupy it.
 Then other would-be successors ran out of patience. First, tech mogul, Justice Democrats co-founder, and AOC chief of staff Saikat Chakrabarti declared for the seat in October 2025. He was quickly followed by Wiener , with both entering the fray before the former Speaker had publicly announced her retirement. This formidable field chased Christine Pelosi out of the race and, by all accounts, deeply annoyed her mom, who felt disrespected by the rush to force her to step down. Before the June 2 primary, Nancy Pelosi decided to back a third candidate, San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan , a more conventional liberal than either Chakrabarti or Wiener.
 In the primary, the well-known Wiener finished first and Chan second with Chakrabarti being the odd candidate out. But the ensuing general election took on a whole new dimension when Wiener got some high-life money and backing from one faction of an AI industry that haunts San Francisco like a rich but demanding uncle.
 Even as the Abundance Agenda was filled out by doers and thinkers who viewed Wiener as an inspiring figure, he had established a strong foothold in the AI-safety movement and its philosophical allies in the effective-altruism community, both closely associated with Anthropic. Wiener and New York legislator Alex Bores had become West and East Coast anchors of a group of state legislators committed to AI-safety measures who privately coordinated with each other on AI policy and how to handle pressure from industry lobbyists.
 Bores’s congressional campaign in Manhattan became a national lightning rod and proxy war for battling schools of thought in the AI industry . An Anthropic-funded AI-safety-focused PAC (Public First Action) spent $12 million to back him, and a rival AI PAC opposing state regulation (Leading the Future, funded by big dogs representing OpenAI and the AI investor Andreessen Horowitz) spent $8 million to defeat him. In the end, Bores narrowly lost the Democratic primary to Micah Lasher . Restlessly looking for another champion in Congress, Public First Action decided to go big on Wiener, tossing $3 million into his campaign in mid-October. That gave the already well-funded legislator a crucial home-stretch advantage over Chan, who had lots of endorsements (from Pelosi, Senator Adam Schiff , and most unions) but not much dough.
 As Wiener and Chan battled for votes, however, his relationship with AI firms became the campaign’s central issue with Wiener touting himself as an AI-safety watchdog of the industry and Chan and her allies labeling him a lapdog . Fortunately for Wiener, the Anthropic rivals who helped take down Bores did not get involved in the race; nor did Pelosi fix her candidate up with the resources necessary to win. Wiener ultimately defeated Chan by just over 6 percent of the vote.
 Despite all the attacks on Wiener for both his up-zoning initiatives and his AI friends, he’d be considered a pretty rigorous progressive anywhere other than San Francisco. He was endorsed by the California Democratic Party, after all, and his actual campaign (rather than the shadow campaign that dwelled on his associations) focused on pledges to honor Pelosi’s legacy and fight Donald Trump tooth and nail. After Chan conceded the race, Pelosi pledged cooperation with Wiener, and in a final touch of irony, Christine Pelosi announced her candidacy for Wiener’s soon-to-be-vacated state-senate seat (though Wiener himself endorsed his Sacramento legislative ally Matt Haney).
 Meanwhile, Nancy Pelosi’s successor is heading to Washington as an iconic figure in two separate movements that could be near and dear to the hearts of centrist Democrats going forward: the Abundance Agenda and the effort to thread the needle on AI via safety and guideline measures that regulate the industry without putting it down like the rabid beast so many progressives fear it has become.
 That a man like Wiener will represent San Francisco in Congress is the product of both the perceived excesses of the city’s fractious progressive groups during their long dominance of the city’s political culture and the complex influence of the tech industry, which includes but transcends AI. More generally, San Francisco reflects California in its ambivalence toward the immensely powerful and wealthy spawn of Silicon Valley. Even as Wiener won the battle to succeed Pelosi with backing from some (but not all) tech titans, other tech titans massively funded the successful effort to defeat Proposition 40 , the billionaire tax backed by Bernie Sanders and his allies but opposed by most of California’s leading Democrats. While the blue wave said a lot about what voters care about nationally, the upheaval that played out in San Francisco reflects the shifting tectonics of this Democratic-dominated but ideologically diverse state. It’s not entirely the Left Coast any more.
